items.stem: In ASP.NET Core MVC, why does the model not depend on the view or controller?

options.text: So the model can be built and tested independently of presentation
options.rationale: Correct: one-way dependency is a key benefit of the separation.

options.text: Because the model is written in a different language
options.rationale: All three are typically C#; the point is dependency direction.
Views do use models; the model just does not depend on them.

items.explanation: Correct: one-way dependency is a key benefit of the separation.

items.stem: Which TWO are benefits of a dedicated view model over using the business model in the view? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The view can vary independently of the business/data model
options.rationale: Correct: separation lets presentation change without touching business types.

options.text: It limits what data is exposed to the view and to model binding
options.rationale: Correct: a view model offers a security and shaping benefit.

options.text: It removes the need for any model binding
options.rationale: Model binding is still used with view models.
View models are commonly where validation attributes live.

items.explanation: Correct: separation lets presentation change without touching business types.

items.stem: A posted form fails validation. What should the action typically do?

options.text: Return the view with the invalid ModelState so errors show
options.rationale: Correct: redisplaying the view with ModelState surfaces validation errors.
Validation failure is expected flow, not an exception to crash on.

options.text: Ignore the errors and redirect to success
options.rationale: Ignoring errors stores or confirms bad data.

items.explanation: Correct: redisplaying the view with ModelState surfaces validation errors.
